title: Rhythm & Gash (Pt. 1)
artist: Rebound X (RBX; real name given by RA as Benjamin Darroux)
label: White label (per RA)
format: Uncertain: RA (2020) files it as a white-label single but also says the track appeared on the 2006 EP 'Land Of X', his only release
tracklist_note: RA lists a single track, 'Rhythm & Gash Pt. 1'. RA says it appeared on the 2006 EP 'Land Of X'; no tracklist for that EP was found.

sound_descriptions.text: RA (2020) describes a bouncy, traditional eight-bar grime structure with a very impactful drop, a heaving drums-and-bass push and a diva-style vocal sample; a source quoted by RA calls it 'a really unique way of using a vocal sample'.
Complex (Joseph JP Patterson, April 2016) calls it a lyric-free, 'rolling, bass-bouncing' and haunting riddim.

context.text: RA (Carlos Hawthorn, 'Rewind', 20 Nov 2020): Rebound X posted on the RWD and VIP2 forums and appears to have left the internet around 2008; Mr. Mitch said the tune 'didn't really get no love' when first shared on the forums; some say it was never registered with PRS.

RA says Skepta named it 'tune of the month' on a 2007 Rinse FM recording and that Skepta and JME's 'Spaceship Freestyle' was the turning point; DJ Logan Sama describes it as a dependable call-and-response dancefloor record.
VICE (Josh Baines, 27 Nov 2015): Elijah of Butterz suggests it may be the biggest grime instrumental, says it 'came out back in 2006', and notes DJ EZ playing Flava D's remix revived it.
Complex (2016) quotes Faze Miyake calling it 'one of the most universal grime tunes out' and Plastician saying its popularity may not yet have peaked.

relationships.other: Skepta and JME - 'Spaceship Freestyle' (2007)
Tempa T and President T vocal versions (Complex places these about two years after 2007)
Skepta with Jammer - 'I Spy' (per Complex 2016)
Sir Spyro remix; Murlo remix; Flava D 4x4 edit/remix (DJ EZ support)

uncertainty: Release format is unclear: RA labels it a white-label single but also says it appeared on the 2006 'Land Of X' EP. No catalogue number or label name was found. The 2006 date rests on RA (2020) and VICE (2015); Complex's 2016 piece says it was 'ten years after its initial release' in 2015, which roughly agrees. Discogs was not reachable.

Complex's 25 best Skepta songs says it was originally released in 2006, appeared on Greatest Hits the following year, and cemented Skepta's reputation 'as both MC and producer'.
Stereogum calls it one of the last grime anthems of the early-to-mid 2000s.

title: Grime 2
label: Rephlex
format: Compilation (format not stated in sources opened; XLR8R says nine tracks)
tracklist_note: XLR8R gives nine tracks without titles. Kode9's own Bandcamp reissue of his tracks from the comp lists 'Dislokated', 'Ping', 'Sub Kontinent' and 'Swarm'. RA (2021) says Digital Mystikz's 'CR7 Chamber' first appeared on Grime 2.

sound_descriptions.text: The Brooklyn Rail (Dominic Umile, June 2010) describes Kode9's four tracks as crude and wordless, mixing film dialogue and Eastern reed instruments with heavy bass lines, with no vocalists.
XLR8R (Brion Paul, July 2005) points to Eastern-tinged hip-hop touches, acoustic-guitar R&B smoothness and jungle-style 'precision bass blasts'.
RA (Emeka Okonkwo, 2021) calls Digital Mystikz's 'CR7 Chamber' 'dark and glacial'.

context.text: Rephlex Records discography (Wikipedia mirror) lists CAT 156 'Grime' and CAT 160 'Grime 2' as consecutive various-artist releases.
The Brooklyn Rail says Rephlex 'understandably misidentified' the music as grime, and links the comp to the infancy of what became dubstep.
RA says CR7 Chamber was among the tracks that first hooked audiences, and the duo stayed underground until DJs worldwide noticed in 2006.

Comments under k-punk's April 2004 post on the first Rephlex 'Grime' comp were already disputing whether the FWD/dubstep producers and the MC-led grime scene were the same thing; Hyperdub's steve_hyperdub says Slaughter Mob saw themselves as dubstep.

relationships.other: Rephlex - Grime (CAT 156, 2004), already in register as rephlex-grime-comp-cat156-2004
Kode9 - 'trax from Grime 2 [2004]' (Bandcamp digital, 22 March 2020)
Digital Mystikz - 'CR7 Chamber' digital reissue on DMZ (August 2021)

uncertainty: No exact release date or physical format was confirmed. The 2004 year comes from Kode9's Bandcamp and RA; XLR8R's review is dated July 2005. Genre is contested: the label titled it 'Grime', but later writers treat it as early dubstep. It is included as evidence of how the grime label was applied in 2004.

title: Morgue
format: Physical record sold through East London shops and from Wiley's car boot (per Slimzee); exact format not stated
tracklist_note: Slimzee says Roll Deep (including Riko, Wiley, Scratchy and Trim) did a vocal; whether the vocal and instrumental were on the same record is not stated.

sound_descriptions.text: Slimzee (Quietus Baker's Dozen, 2023) describes an unusual half-time feel that was 'just so gritty', and says Wiley made it as a version of DJ Wonder's 'What'.

context.text: Slimzee says Wiley sold it for a tenner though it cost about 50p to make, that shops bought it by the box, and that it was sold under the counter after Geeneus threatened to withhold Dump Valve tunes from shops stocking what he saw as a bootleg of 'What'.
District Magazine (Cóilí Collins, 7 July 2017) lists it among five grime instrumentals that helped shape the genre, noting its later use for Skepta's diss 'Nasty'.
Included in Son Raw's 'Classic Grime Riddims' mix (Music Is My Sanctuary, October 2014).

sound_descriptions.text: In FACT (2009), Simon Reynolds calls the synth on the Frontline remix 'harmonically rich'. Terror says it is a normal synth that he processes and textures heavily, and he declines to explain how.
Planet Mu (2009) describes Terror Danjah's style as a small set of signature sounds, shifting syncopated rhythms, around 140 bpm, and a gremlin-cackle audio logo.

context.text: Terror Danjah tells FACT that Payback was 'one of Aftershock's top sellers', especially the Frontline remix, and places it after the Industry Standard EP (2004).

The Aftershock (group) Wikipedia article lists Payback as a 2004 various-artist remix EP and repeats that it was one of the label's top sellers. It describes the original 'Frontline' (2003) as Big E-D featuring D Double E.
FACT: Big E.D.'s 'Frontline' followed Crazy Titch's 'I Can C U' and N.A.S.T.Y.'s 'Cock Back' as an early Aftershock release.
